Binary search finds a target value in a **sorted** list by repeatedly halving the search interval. It compares the target to the middle element; if they match, it’s done. If the target is smaller, the algorithm discards the upper half, otherwise it discards the lower half, and repeats the process on the remaining half until the target is found or the interval is empty—giving a worst‑case time complexity of O(log n).

Binary search finds a target value in a sorted list by repeatedly halving the search interval. Start with the whole list, compare the target to the middle element, and then discard the half that cannot contain the target—if the target is smaller, keep the left half; if larger, keep the right half. Repeat this step on the remaining sub‑list until the target is found or the interval is empty. Because the list size shrinks by a factor of two each iteration, the worst‑case time is O(log n) and the algorithm uses only O(1) extra space.
